SKM-SPN-0001.title: Advanced clinical reasoning — Sciatica / Lumbosacral Radicular Pain
principles: Do not diagnose the level from pain location alone. Localize using the combined pattern of pain, sensory change, motor weakness, reflex change and provocative testing.
Pain severity and neurological severity are separate. Severe pain can occur without major motor deficit; a relatively painless foot drop can still be neurologically important.
Straight Leg Raise (SLR) angle is not a validated standalone severity grade and must not by itself determine X-ray or MRI.

slr.meaning: Very early reproduction can indicate marked neural irritability, but is not specific and is NOT automatically 'severe disc prolapse'. Recheck technique and consider hip pathology, non-neural pain, extreme irritability or other causes.
slr.action: Correlate with dermatomal pain, motor/sensory/reflex findings and red flags.

slr.meaning: Classical positive zone when concordant radicular pain is reproduced down the posterior/lateral leg, typically below the knee. Most useful for lower lumbar L5/S1 nerve-root irritation.
slr.action: Document side, angle, exact pain path and whether ankle dorsiflexion sensitizes symptoms.

slr.meaning: Pain appearing only at higher hip-flexion angles is generally less specific for nerve-root tension; hamstring, hip/SI or local musculoskeletal sources become more important differentials.
slr.action: Do not label as radiculopathy from SLR alone.

slr.meaning: Raising the asymptomatic leg reproduces the symptomatic-leg radicular pain. Less sensitive but more specific for disc herniation/root compression than ipsilateral SLR.
slr.action: Raises confidence when the rest of the clinical picture is concordant.

severity.interpretation: Pain score measures symptom burden, not neurological urgency.

severity.severe: ≤3/5, new foot drop or progressive weakness
severity.interpretation: Progressive or major objective weakness deserves expedited MRI/specialist assessment.

severity.moderate: Reduced walking, sitting or work tolerance
severity.severe: Unable to heel/toe walk, repeated falls, marked gait deterioration
severity.interpretation: Functional loss helps grade clinical impact.

severity.severe: New bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle sensory loss, bilateral major deficit
severity.interpretation: Cauda equina pathway → urgent MRI/emergency spine assessment.

localization.commonDisc: Usually L3–L4 paracentral/traversing L4; L4–L5 far-lateral can affect exiting L4
localization.motor: Knee extension (quadriceps); ankle dorsiflexion may contribute
localization.gait: Knee buckling; heel walking may be impaired if dorsiflexion involved
localization.pearls: Femoral stretch test is more useful than SLR for upper/midlumbar L2–L4 roots.

localization.commonDisc: L4–L5 paracentral/lateral recess commonly affects traversing L5; L5–S1 far-lateral may affect exiting L5
localization.pain: Buttock/lateral thigh → anterolateral leg → dorsum foot/great toe
localization.motor: Great-toe extension (EHL), ankle dorsiflexion, hip abduction; eversion may weaken
localization.reflex: No consistently reliable routine deep tendon reflex; compare overall exam
localization.gait: Heel walking difficulty; toe drag; foot drop is classically L5-predominant but consider common peroneal neuropathy
localization.pearls: Weak inversion suggests L5 radiculopathy more than isolated common-peroneal neuropathy.

localization.commonDisc: L5–S1 paracentral/lateral recess commonly affects traversing S1
localization.pain: Buttock/posterior thigh → posterior calf → lateral foot/sole
localization.motor: Plantar flexion (gastrocnemius/soleus), hip extension/knee flexion may contribute
localization.gait: Toe walking or repeated single-leg heel raises impaired
localization.pearls: Unable to perform repeated heel raises strongly supports clinically important S1 motor dysfunction when concordant.

symptomCorrelation.meaning: Supports radicular pain when it follows a root-related leg distribution, especially below the knee.
symptomCorrelation.next: Map exact path; distinguish from referred pain.

symptomCorrelation.meaning: Suggests sensory nerve-root irritation but is not level-specific alone.
symptomCorrelation.next: Map dermatome and compare pinprick/light touch sides.

symptomCorrelation.meaning: Objective sensory loss carries more localization value than vague tingling.
symptomCorrelation.next: Document L4 medial ankle, L5 great toe/dorsum, S1 lateral foot/sole tendencies.

symptomCorrelation.meaning: Myotomal weakness is more clinically important than pain intensity.
symptomCorrelation.next: MRC-grade key muscles and repeat over time.

symptomCorrelation.meaning: Most often L5-predominant radiculopathy or common peroneal neuropathy; central causes also possible.
symptomCorrelation.next: Test dorsiflexion, EHL, inversion, eversion; inspect sensory pattern and reflexes; expedited imaging if acute/progressive.

symptomCorrelation.meaning: Suggests dorsiflexor weakness, commonly L4/L5 (especially L5 clinical pattern).
symptomCorrelation.next: Correlate with EHL, tibialis anterior and L5 sensory findings.
Compare Achilles reflex and lateral-foot sensation.

imagingDecision.scenario: Acute uncomplicated radicular pain, no red flags, no objective progressive deficit
imagingDecision.why: Routine imaging rarely changes early management and degenerative abnormalities are common incidentally.

imagingDecision.scenario: Low-velocity/significant trauma, osteoporosis, older age, chronic steroid exposure
imagingDecision.test: Lumbar radiographs (AP & Lateral) and/or CT/MRI according to suspected fracture
imagingDecision.why: Bony fracture risk changes the imaging pathway.

imagingDecision.scenario: Persistent/progressive radiculopathy after ~6 weeks of appropriate management and patient is intervention/surgery candidate
imagingDecision.why: Defines disc/root compression when the result is expected to change management.

imagingDecision.scenario: New/progressive objective motor deficit, clinically important foot drop
imagingDecision.why: Neurological progression matters more than pain score or SLR angle.
imagingDecision.priority: RED/AMBER depending on progression and severity

imagingDecision.scenario: Cauda equina symptoms: bladder/bowel/saddle change, severe bilateral deficits
imagingDecision.why: Time-sensitive neural compression must be excluded.

imagingDecision.test: MRI ± contrast and targeted laboratory workup
imagingDecision.why: Alternative serious pathology requires a different diagnostic pathway.

medEvidence.role: May be considered for symptom relief
medEvidence.evidence: NICE notes limited evidence of benefit in sciatica and emphasizes harms; if used, lowest effective dose for shortest period.

medEvidence.role: Not a 'latest sciatica-specific' drug. Evidence exists for chronic non-radicular low-back pain; choice is individualized and region/label dependent.
medEvidence.evidence: Etoricoxib 60 mg/day was comparable with diclofenac 150 mg/day in an older chronic low-back-pain RCT. COX-2 cardiovascular/renal/BP risk remains important.

medEvidence.role: Do NOT add as routine sciatica prescription simply because pain is neuropathic.
medEvidence.evidence: Large placebo-controlled sciatica trial found no significant benefit and more adverse events; NICE recommends not offering gabapentinoids for sciatica.

medEvidence.role: Do NOT add as routine sciatica prescription.
medEvidence.evidence: NICE groups gabapentinoids/antiepileptics as not recommended for sciatica due lack of overall benefit and harm.
RCT of a 15-day prednisone taper showed modest functional improvement but no significant pain benefit; NICE advises not to offer oral corticosteroids for sciatica.

medEvidence.role: May have a role in selected acute non-radicular low-back pain with spasm under some guidelines, but evidence is not established for sciatica itself.
medEvidence.evidence: Do not automatically carry non-radicular LBP recommendations into nerve-root sciatica.

medEvidence.role: Treat documented or strongly suspected deficiency; not a routine treatment for mechanical nerve-root compression.
medEvidence.evidence: Useful when B12 deficiency/neuropathy is present, but does not decompress a nerve root.

decisionPearls: A low SLR angle can mean high irritability, but a patient with 60° SLR and MRC 3/5 foot dorsiflexion is neurologically more concerning than a patient with 25° painful SLR but full power and no red flags.
MRI must answer a clinical question: does the side/level/morphology explain the neurological pattern and will the result change management?
A paracentral L4–L5 disc usually affects the traversing L5 root; a paracentral L5–S1 disc usually affects S1. Far-lateral lesions usually affect the exiting root.
Foot drop requires localization: L5 radiculopathy versus common peroneal neuropathy versus plexus/central causes.
World-class clinical reasoning means knowing when NOT to order imaging and when NOT to prescribe a commonly used drug.

SKM-LSP-0002.title: Advanced reasoning — Mechanical / Non-specific Low Back Pain
principles: Confirm absence of radiculopathy and red flags before calling pain non-specific.
Use function, duration, neurological screen and psychosocial recovery factors rather than imaging abnormalities to grade clinical importance.
decisionPearls: A small disc bulge on MRI does not convert non-specific low-back pain into discogenic disease without concordant clinical evidence.
Routine X-ray/MRI is not a marker of thoroughness in uncomplicated low-back pain.

imagingDecision.scenario: Persistent/progressive symptoms >~6 weeks with intervention consideration

SKM-LSP-0003.title: Advanced reasoning — Lumbar Disc Herniation / PIVD
principles: Disc morphology must be matched to root level, side and neurological examination.
Protrusion/extrusion/sequestration describes morphology; clinical urgency is determined more by neurological compromise and red flags than by the word used in the MRI report.
decisionPearls: Paracentral L4–L5 → usually traversing L5; paracentral L5–S1 → usually S1.
Far-lateral L4–L5 → exiting L4; far-lateral L5–S1 → exiting L5.
Crossed SLR is particularly useful when positive because of higher specificity for disc herniation.

imagingDecision.scenario: Typical acute radiculopathy without deficit/red flag

imagingDecision.why: Emergency decompression pathway may be needed.

SKM-LSP-0004.title: Advanced reasoning — Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
principles: Clinical neurogenic claudication requires posture-/walking-related symptoms; MRI stenosis alone is not the diagnosis.
Differentiate vascular claudication using pulses, vascular risk, symptom relation to posture and ABI when appropriate.
decisionPearls: Shopping-cart/flexion relief supports neurogenic claudication but is not individually diagnostic.
Walking tolerance and function often matter more than static canal measurements.

imagingDecision.scenario: Concordant neurogenic claudication with intervention consideration

SKM-CSP-0001.title: Advanced reasoning — Cervical Radiculopathy
principles: Separate radiculopathy from myelopathy before focusing on root-level treatment.
Combine dermatomal symptoms, myotomal weakness, reflex change, Spurling/ULTT and shoulder/peripheral-nerve differentiation.
decisionPearls: Spurling is a rule-in style provocative test when concordant; ULTT is useful as a more sensitive neurodynamic test.
Gait imbalance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia or leg stiffness shifts the problem from 'root' to possible 'cord' and increases urgency.

imagingDecision.scenario: Typical short-duration radiculopathy without red flags
Persistent symptoms ~4–6 weeks or objective progressive deficit
imagingDecision.why: Defines root compression and changes interventional/surgical planning.
